title: Easter Sunday
hook: the tomb is empty and the alleluia returns

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Exsultet, and the whole Bible story read by candlelight. Your line was the whole story in one night.

Since Ash Wednesday, a single word has been missing from the Mass. Not dropped by accident: put away. In some places, children even wrote it on a banner before Lent and buried it in the churchyard. All through Lent the Gospel was greeted with other words. Then last night, after the readings, the priest sang it three times, each time a little higher, and the people sang it back. This morning it's everywhere: on the doors, in the hymns, doubled at the end of Mass.
screen: `ALL LENT WITHOUT IT.` → `SUNG THREE TIMES, RISING.` → `EASTER MORNING.`

segments.voice: Start with the morning Gospel. On Easter Sunday the Church reads John. Mary Magdalene comes to the tomb while it's still dark and finds the stone rolled away. She runs to Peter and the other disciple, the one Jesus loved, and the two of them race back. The other disciple outruns Peter, gets there first, looks in, and waits. Peter goes straight in and sees the linen cloths lying there, and the face cloth rolled up by itself. Then the other disciple goes in, and John says he saw and believed. No angel's speech, no appearance yet. Just two out-of-breath men and an empty room. Matthew puts it in an angel's mouth, in the Douay-Rheims: "He is not here, for he is risen, as he said." Now the word. Alleluia is Hebrew: hallelu, praise, plural, all of you, and Yah, the short form of God's name. Praise the Lord, everybody. It opens and closes a run of Psalms, and the Book of Revelation has heaven singing it. The Church buried it for Lent so that it could come back like this. Today the dismissal at the end of Mass gets a double alleluia, and it will keep it through the eight days of the octave and again at Pentecost. Some Catholics also use a greeting from the Christian East this morning: one person says Christ is risen, and the other answers, he is risen indeed. Christians say the tomb was empty because he was raised, and Paul writes that if Christ is not risen, their preaching is in vain. A great deal rests on that empty room.
screen: `TWO DISCIPLES RACE TO THE TOMB.` · `HE SAW AND BELIEVED.` · `HALLELU-YAH: PRAISE THE LORD.` · `BURIED FOR LENT, BACK TODAY.` · then, large: `HE IS NOT HERE, FOR HE IS RISEN.`

segments.voice: Picture someone to tell, a parent, a friend, someone at Mass, a group chat, and say it to them quietly in whatever words fit: Christ is risen, or happy Easter, or simply alleluia. If those aren't your words, picture the women running from the tomb, and notice what good news does to a body.
Easter Sunday. The morning of the empty tomb, when the alleluia comes back after Lent. Today's word.
Your line: alleluia. Praise the Lord, everybody, sung again after the long quiet of Lent. Happy Easter.

howItsDone: On Easter Sunday Catholics celebrate Mass with the Gospel of the empty tomb, sing the alleluia that was silent through Lent, end Mass with a double alleluia, and often greet each other with Christ is risen and the answer he is risen indeed.

chat.says: What does alleluia actually mean? I hear it everywhere at Easter.
options: Hebrew for praise the Lord, all of you: hallelu plus Yah, God's name.
It's Latin for he is risen, the greeting people say at Easter.
It's Greek for joy, a word the first Christians made up for Easter.
chat.meaning: Alleluia is Hebrew: hallelu, praise, said to all of you, and Yah, the short form of God's name. Praise the Lord, everybody.

notes: 'Burying the alleluia' banner custom: a medieval and modern custom in some places; framed as 'in some places'.
Double alleluia at the dismissal: through the Easter octave and on Pentecost (Missal); confirm.
Solemn alleluia at the Vigil intoned by the priest three times, raising the pitch; confirm.
The paschal greeting 'Christ is risen / he is risen indeed' attributed to Eastern Christian usage; confirm phrasing.
Psalm references for alleluia given in Hebrew numbering; Douay numbering differs.
